inline.s: Before long the Junior Master-ancestor also passed away, and from that time on there was no one left to sustain the legacy of Monk Xilin. Because Xilin had been in the habit of keeping no savings, every expense of the funeral had to be borrowed, and so a great many debts were incurred. If the temple's property were taken to repay them, this famous monastery south of the Yangtze would be ruined in a single morning. At this point the Master recalled Xilin's charge and resolved to protect the temple's property. He found ways to repay every loan, and what remained he used to maintain the life of the monastery; only thus was the Temple of Requital of Kindness preserved.

That winter Master Hanshan went to Tianjie Temple to hear Master Wuji expound the Lotus Sutra. Because he had set his heart on a pilgrimage of study, he kept watching during the lectures for one among the monks whose precepts and practice were both excellent, to be his companion on the road; but a long time passed, and he never found a fellow traveler after his heart.
One day the Master went to the latrine
(the privy)
, and found it spotlessly clean. He thought: this latrine keeper
(the monk in charge of cleaning the latrines)
must be no ordinary man. So he went to the guest quarters to call on him. When he saw him, he was a man jaundiced and swollen, which made him all the more puzzled.

Every morning when the Master rose and went to the latrine, he always found it already swept spotlessly clean, and never knew when the cleaning had been done. Wishing to find out, one evening after the day's practice had ended he walked up and down the corridor, secretly watching the latrine keeper. He saw that by the time the assembly was dismissed, the man had already finished tidying the latrine. Several days later the Master noticed that the latrine was no longer clean and that the keeper did not appear; on inquiring of the monastic officers, he learned that the latrine keeper had fallen ill in the guest quarters. The Master went at once to visit him, and seeing that the illness was grave, asked with concern: “Master, how does your body feel? Are body and mind still at peace?” The latrine keeper answered: “This body is so bound by karmic obstruction that I can scarcely hold up, and the thought of craving food is even harder to bear.” The Master asked him why. He said: “When I see everyone taking their meal, my mind can never let go of the thought of eating.” The Master laughed and said: “That is the hunger of long illness.” From this encounter the Master knew that the man was a genuine practitioner; so he went back and prepared some fruit and cakes to bring to him, and asked him his Dharma name. The latrine keeper replied: “My secular surname is Xu; I am a descendant of Xu Juju of the Spring and Autumn period. My home is in Puzhou, and my Dharma name is now Miaofeng.” The Master at once proposed that they join company and travel on pilgrimage, and Miaofeng gladly agreed, saying to the Master: “If you have this resolve, then on the road I will carry your straw sandals for you, and when we settle on a mountain I will supply you with firewood and water.” Before long Miaofeng recovered; but when the Master went to see him again, he had long since vanished. The Master understood that, his great matter of investigation still unfinished, he feared to be encumbered, and so had slipped quietly away.
[Miaofeng]
The Annotated Chronicle of Master Hanshan records:
“Master Miaofeng of Puzhou, whose name was Fudeng, went to Nanhai to offer incense on behalf of the Prince of Shanyin. On his way back he passed through Jianye
(Nanjing)
, and as a northerner newly come to the south he was afflicted by dampness and broke out in sores; so he asked at the Tianjie monastery for the post of latrine keeper, as a way to rest.”
, the Master was twenty-two. That year the education authorities issued a proclamation establishing a charity school at the Temple of Requital of Kindness
(a charity school, where poor children studied free of charge)

, for the express training of monks. Master Hanshan was invited to serve as the teacher, and two hundred young monks came to study under him. The Master therefore went back over the writings of the various masters and the hundred schools, the Zuo Commentary, the Records of the Grand Historian, and other works, devoting himself to the work of education. The following year Gaozuo Temple also invited the Master to teach there, and for the two years after that he was engaged to lecture at Jinshan Temple. In all, the four years from his twenty-second to his twenty-fifth year were spent in the bustle of educating monks.

blocks.text: 5. Wandering Afar in Search of Learning

inline.s: In the fifth year of Longqing (

), Master Hanshan was twenty-six. He set out with Dharma Master Xuelang on a study journey to Mount Lu. When they reached Nankang the local people told them that tigers were causing trouble in the mountains and that it was unsafe to climb, so braving wind and snow they made their way to Ji'an and paid their respects at Qingyuan Temple.

The Master saw that Qingyuan Temple had fallen into such decay that it was painful to look at: the monastic rules had long been lost, and the monks had all grown their hair and beards. He was filled with deep lament and resolved to restore the temple. He therefore advised those in charge to select men under forty who were willing to leave home and cultivate, and to ordain them as monks; more than forty were obtained. At the same time he reorganized the monks already in the temple. From then on Qingyuan Temple regained its former state, and a pure and clean Sangha was established.

When summer came, the Master returned from Qingyuan Temple to the Temple of Requital of Kindness to attend to its affairs. By the time he had set everything in order it was already the eleventh month, and only then did he begin preparing to fulfill his vow of traveling far with a single bowl. Dharma Master Xuelang objected, fearing that he could not endure the hardship and cold of a long journey, and urged him first to travel in Zhejiang and Jiangsu, where the climate was mild and there were many beautiful mountains and waters and lovely scenery to enjoy. But the Master held: “The habitual tendencies of us living beings all cling to softness and ease, and delight in scenery that pleases the eye and gladdens the heart. If one wants to end birth and death and cut off afflictions, one must train hard and go where the habits have no room to run wild; only there is it easy to subdue the afflictions and habits. If I merely linger in the regions of Jiangsu and Zhejiang, is that not as close as the mat and pillow? What meaning would that have for cultivation?” Xuelang, however, insisted that he must not go, and pressed him to stay. But Master Hanshan's resolve was fixed, so he deceived Xuelang by saying that he was going into the city, and set out in heavy snow. When Xuelang discovered that the Master had gone and would not return, he wept bitterly for a long time.

The next year the Master came on foot, alone, to Yangzhou. Held up by heavy snow and stricken with illness, he could only stay there for a time. After some days, feeling that his illness had improved, he took up his bowl and went to beg in the marketplace. But when he came to people's doors he could only pace back and forth, unable to call out for alms. The Master wondered what the reason could be. Feeling in his purse, he found that he still had two qian of silver, and he at once examined himself: “So there is still this silver to lean on — that is why I cannot let go.” Just then he saw some monks in the snow begging and getting no food; without hesitation he invited them to an inn, took out all his silver, and ate his fill with them.

The next day the Master went out to beg again. Coming to the door of one or two households, he called out for alms quite naturally, and so received food. He thought to himself with secret joy: “My strength is enough to make light of a minister's stipend of ten thousand bushels.” He therefore had engraved on his bowl the inscription “An Instrument That Makes Light of Ten Thousand Bushels,” and called his patched robe “The Thing That Makes Light of All Under Heaven,” composing an inscription for it as well: “Your form you lend to me, my mind I lend to you; by you this single body is made whole and true, and by you all ten thousand things are counted few. Soon I shall trail these sleeves that catch the long wind's flight, and wear a collar of white cloud light. I rise as soars the swan upon its wing; I rest as hides the dragon in its spring. At ease through all the universe I roam, in mountains and in forests make my home. Why flaunt the scarlet and the purple's glow? I prize alone what frost and snow can never invade.” In this inscription the Master fully expressed his indifferent temper and his lofty, pure aspiration.
In the seventh month of that year the Master arrived in the capital
(Yanjing, present-day Beijing)

, and having nowhere to lodge, he could only beg in the streets from morning to night; yet by dusk he had not obtained a morsel of food. As darkness fell he came to the tea shed at West Taipingcang, and only there received one meal. That night he slept at Yijiao Temple by the river nearby.

Wang Boyu, elder brother of the Master's youthful schoolmate Wang Zhongyan, was at this time Left Vice Minister of War. Hearing that the Master had come to the capital, he invited him to stay at his house for ten days. Afterwards the Master paid his respects to Chan Master Mohe Zhong, and followed Master Zhong to the Western Hills to hear the Miaozong Chao. When the lecture period ended, Master Zhong kept him for the winter, and he received instruction in the Lotus Sutra and the Cheng Weishi Lun; and he asked Dharma Master An to explain hetuvidyā
(one of the five sciences, namely logic)
and its three-membered syllogism.
One day in the eleventh month there came to the Western Hills a man with long hair, wearing a brown robe
(coarse cloth garments, such as the poor and lowly wore in ancient times)

. He stood before the Master's door and first called out loudly: “A salt merchant has come to visit!” Then he walked straight in. As soon as he saw the Master he asked: “Do you still recognize me?” The Master looked him over carefully for a while, and when he saw those bright, piercing eyes he suddenly recalled the monk Miaofeng who had been latrine keeper at Tianjie Temple, and said: “I recognize you.” Miaofeng said wittily: “I have changed my head and face!” The Master answered with humor too: “The original face is still there, at ease as ever!” The two looked at each other and smiled.

The next day Master Miaofeng came to pay his respects. At night the two sat cross-legged and talked heart to heart, and the Master asked him why he was dressed in that way. Master Miaofeng answered: “I am now living at Longhua Temple in Shanyin. Because I have long dwelt among the mountains, my hair and beard have grown and I have no way to cut them. Not long ago the patron Prince of Shanyin was building a temple, and he asked me to obtain a set of the canon; that is why I have come here. What brings you here too?” Master Hanshan said: “First, I came north to look for you; second, I wished to see the capital and call upon the good and wise teachers of the realm, so as to cut off the delusive hope of regretting in days to come that I had not met them.” Master Miaofeng said: “Since we parted, there has not been a moment when I did not think of you, and sometimes I thought we should never meet again. How fortunate that you have come here, and that we have this one meeting,” and so they talked the whole night through. The next morning they parted with a smile.

Master Hanshan then went alone to pay his respects to Master Bianrong. Having entered and made prostration, he respectfully asked Master Bianrong to point out the practice of the one step beyond. Master Bianrong said not a word, only fixing both eyes on him. Then the Master went to pay his respects to Chan Master Xiaoyan. The Chan master asked: “Where have you come from?” The Master answered: “From the south.” The Chan master asked again: “Do you remember the road by which you came?” The Master said: “Once I have passed it, I pay it no more heed!” The Chan master praised him: “Yet your place of coming is clear!” The Master then bowed his head to the feet of Chan Master Xiaoyan
(touching one's head to the feet of a venerable one — the highest gesture of respect in Buddhism)
, and then stood at his side to ask for instruction. Chan Master Xiaoyan gave him a few words of Dharma on the one step beyond.
Wanli
(the reign title of Emperor Shenzong of the Ming, who came to the throne at the age of ten,
— the era name was changed, and the Master was twenty-eight. At this time he thought of going to Mount Wutai to study, and so first sought out a copy of the Record of the Cool and Clear Mountain
(one of the nine gazetteers of Mount Wutai)

, and by the events and locations recorded in it he decided the direction of his ascent. It was the season when the breath of spring first stirred, and the Master climbed the North Terrace first. Because he knew that the surroundings of Hanshan were quiet and secluded, he asked along the way about the route to Hanshan. Guided by the monks' directions he came to Hanshan, and seeing the strangely beautiful colors of the mountain he was overjoyed, and secretly took “Hanshan” as his own style name. The style name “Hanshan,” by which later generations commonly knew him, dates from this. At this time the Master also wrote a poem expressing his resolve to cultivate on Mount Wutai. Two lines of it run: “Zhemo
(that is, do not)
follow others away; here let me still the workings of the mind.”
[Changing the Era Name]
When a sovereign or a dynasty changes the reign title, the first year of each new title is called the ‘prime year.’

The mountain scenery of Hanshan was wonderfully beautiful, but the climate there was bitterly cold, and for the time being he could not settle there to practice; so the Master had to turn back to the capital and set out eastward to study.

blocks.text: 6. First Awakening to Form and Emptiness

inline.s: One day the Master came in his travels to Mount Pan
(northwest of Jixian in Tianjin, an outlying range of the Yan Mountains; a famous mountain east of Beijing, praised as “the first mountain east of the capital”)

, Qianxiang Peak. When he reached the summit of Mount Pan he saw a recluse living beside a rock at the side of the peak, with gray hair and an earth-colored face. The Master went in and bowed to him, but the man did not raise his head, only sitting upright with his mind collected; and when asked anything he did not utter a sound. The Master realized that this recluse was no ordinary man, and so sat down in meditation beside him.

After a while the recluse rose and boiled tea. When the water had boiled he poured himself a cup and drank; seeing this, the Master also poured a cup and drank. When the tea was finished the recluse put the tea things back in their place and, still silent, sat down in meditation again, and the Master did the same. After another while the recluse rose and cooked a meal; when it was ready he filled a bowl and ate by himself, and the Master also filled a bowl and ate with him. After the meal the recluse sat upright as before, and the Master also sat upright. When night came the recluse rose and went outside the rock to walk in meditation, and the Master followed him out and walked too.

The next day the recluse no longer stirred. Following the recluse's times for tea and meals, the Master boiled tea and cooked rice punctually; after the two had eaten they sat in silent investigation as before, and at nightfall they walked together again. Thus they passed seven days in utter silence, until at last the recluse opened his mouth and asked the Master:
Where have you come from?”
From the south.”
What have you come here to do?”
I came especially to visit the recluse.”
The recluse's face is utterly ordinary — what is there that is special?”
I saw through it the moment I stepped in!”
Hearing this the recluse laughed and said: “I have lived here for more than thirty years, and only today have I met a man of the same wind
(a man of like style)
!” So he asked the Master to stay, and the Master, feeling that he had met a man of high attainment from whom he might well learn, stayed on.

One night the Master, as usual, went out before the rock to walk in meditation. In the midst of his walking, suddenly a crash like thunder sounded at the crown of his head. In an instant mountains, rivers, and the great earth, body, mind, and world, were utterly empty. This emptiness was not the “emptiness” of the eye-faculty set over against empty dust, but the state of empty samādhi corresponding to the mind. In this empty samādhi about the time of five inches of incense passed before he slowly became aware of the existence of his body, and slowly felt the solidity of the ground beneath his feet, and opening his eyes slowly saw the mountains and rivers and the great earth again. All the physiological functions of his body returned to what they had been before. His body seemed to be borne up by a wind, light and joyful, and the inner bliss he tasted could not be put into words.

When the Master returned to the cave, the recluse asked him: “You walked in meditation tonight — why did it last so long?” The Master told him one by one the states he had experienced. The recluse gravely warned him: “You are still within the realm of the aggregate of form; that is not your original mind-nature. I have lived here more than thirty years, and except in rain, snow, and wind, every night's walking brings such a state. If you do not dwell upon that state, it will not delude you out of your original mind-nature!” Hearing this, the Master deeply trusted his teaching and bowed in gratitude with great reverence.

Now Master Miaofeng had already obtained the canon, and he asked Wang Boyu where Master Hanshan had gone; Wang Boyu at once sent men up Mount Pan to search. They searched until they came to the cave, and relayed to the Master how urgently Master Miaofeng longed to see him. The Master reflected that he had already stayed long in the cave on Mount Pan, and that he had a prior agreement with Master Miaofeng, so he could not but go. When the Master took his leave of the recluse, neither could bear the parting. The recluse saw him out of the mountain, tears glistening on his face, and accompanied him all the way to the middle of the slope before turning back.

When the Master returned to the capital, Master Miaofeng and Wang Boyu both came out to welcome him. They said to Master Hanshan with a laugh: “Why did you stay so long in the mountains?” The Master then told them the whole story of meeting the recluse in the cave on Mount Pan. When Wang Boyu heard it he said: “Since you have already reached such a state, the matter of dwelling in the mountains may be considered settled!” The Master said: “That is no more than scenery by the roadside; I am still far from the jeweled city!” At this the two looked at each other and burst out laughing.

At that time the capital gathered many eminent men, who were outstanding in virtue and talent and all believers in Buddhism. Such men as the two brothers Wang Fengzhou and Wang Linzhou, the two brothers Wang Boyu and Wang Zhongyan, and Ou Zhenbo of Nanhai were all very famous, and the Master had long admired their virtue and talent.

One day the Master went to visit Wang Fengzhou, who, thinking him young, did not pay him much attention. Seeing how self-important Wang was, the Master too put on a very proud air. Wang instructed him in the method of composing poetry, but the Master merely stared at him with both eyes, and without saying a word got up and left. Wang felt quite put out, and told his younger brother about it. The next day Wang Linzhou came to visit the Master, and the moment they met he said: “Last night my elder brother lost an eye!” The Master said: “Have you an eye, then?” Linzhou clasped his hands in salute and said: “The young fellow has met you face to face!” The two looked at each other and laughed heartily. When Linzhou got home he said to his brother: “Elder brother, you have been worsted by Vimalakīrti.” Later Linzhou wrote a poem to present to the Master, two lines of which read: “We know that Wang Yishao
(Wang Xizhi, whose courtesy name was Yishao)
yielded in metaphysical discourse to Master Zhi
(the eminent Jin-dynasty monk Zhi Dun)

Once, when the Master was together with Wang Zhongyan, who was reading the Zuo Commentary, Wang said to the Master: “You are naturally quick and have great literary talent, and my elder brother is the master craftsman of letters of our day — why do you not study under him, and seek to make a name for yourself as a writer?” The Master laughed and spat, saying: “Keep your elder brother's knees; one day he will bow to this old monk and receive the meaning of the coming from the West
(the essential teaching transmitted by Bodhidharma when he came from the West)

.” Hearing this, Zhongyan was greatly displeased, and when he went back and told Wang Boyu, Boyu said: “I have great faith in him. Looking at his bones of the Way, in time he will enter the inner chambers of Chan Master Dahui and Chan Master Zhongfeng — how could he be willing to be fettered by mere literature? I only fear that his present drifting, superficial wandering in study will ruin the great matter of cultivating the Way!” One day Boyu saw a poem the Master had inscribed on the head of a fan for Zhongyan, and pointing to the two lines “This body and world, a cicada's two wings
tiáo
, the cicada in the ancient books)
, heaven and earth, a horse's single hair,” he said: “Zhongyan, look — how could such a poem have been written by a monk of letters!”

Not long afterwards Wang Boyu prepared a special vegetarian feast to make offerings to Master Hanshan and Master Miaofeng. As they ate they talked, and Boyu said: “The Chan gate is now desolate, with no one to succeed it; this truly deserves our concern, and it is precisely this that weighs on my mind.” Then he said to Master Hanshan: “From your bearing I judge that your future attainment will not be small. Why do you not treasure your time and strive to revive the Chan gate, instead of wandering all over the world?” The Master replied: “This poor monk has come on foot through the world solely for the great matter of birth and death, to call upon good and wise teachers. The reason I now wish to call upon the many great virtuous ones of our time is to cut off the delusive hope of regretting in other days that I had not met them!” Then he added: “I am not wandering idly; I have a purpose, and before long I shall be leaving.” Boyu approved, saying: “I have great faith in what you do. Look at the monks who have left home today — there is not one fit to be your teacher. And but for Master Miaofeng, you would not have found a fellow cultivator to be your Dharma companion.” The Master said: “In the past, amid the assembly at the Dharma gathering, I singled out Master Miaofeng, and at that time we swore an oath to be fellow students; and so I came looking for him, never thinking I should chance upon him here.” Boyu was delighted, and said: “Excellent! If the two of you go to dwell in the mountains and cultivate, I will provide the traveling expenses.”
By this time Master Miaofeng had obtained the canon, and Wang Boyu presented him with the two Kanhe passes; he also wrote an essay and gave it to Master Hanshan.

One day Wang Boyu sent someone to ask the Master to come quickly; the moment they met he said: “Master Miaofeng has already left — why are you still here?” The Master answered: “I thought I would stay a few more days before going.” Boyu was greatly displeased and said: “I know you are unwilling to follow at another's heels, but that is not necessarily right. The ancients were not ashamed of small matters, but ashamed that their merit and name should not be manifest in the world. I hope that in the future you will accomplish a glorious work in the Dharma gate — why, then, weigh such a trifling thing as whether or not to go with another?” The Master was much enlightened by this, thanked him for his good intent, and decided to travel together with Miaofeng. He set out at once to catch up with Miaofeng, and found him already seated in the carriage. Miaofeng asked him: “Brother, are you coming too?” The Master answered: “I am coming too!” and at once climbed into Miaofeng's carriage and departed without taking leave of anyone else.

In the eighth month of autumn, when the sky was high and the air clear, the Master and Miaofeng crossed at Mengjin and viewed the place where King Wu reviewed his troops. Here the Master wrote a poem lamenting the past:
A broken stele and a lonely stone lean on the riverbank; here once he mustered all the lords in ranked array.
The kingly law he established
(the sovereign's guiding order)
should stand as long as heaven and earth, and flow with the Yellow River, unbroken, on and on.
Traveling on to the place where Bo Yi and Shu Qi reined in the horses, the Master wrote another poem lamenting the past:
They cast off throne and glory, their purpose deep and true; only the ancient temple remains, its cypress gloom to view.
So clear the colors of Shouyang Mountain still appear — the very heart that reined the horses in, in that old year.
[Bo Yi and Shu Qi Reining In the Horses]

In the last years of the Shang dynasty, Bo Yi and Shu Qi were sons of the ruler of Guzhu. After the lord of Guzhu died, the two yielded to each other, unwilling to take the throne, and went to King Wen of Zhou. After King Wen died, King Wu sent out his troops to punish the tyrant King Zhou of Shang, carrying King Wen's tablet in the war chariot as he marched. Bo Yi and Shu Qi laid hold of the horses' bridles and remonstrated: “Your father is dead and unburied, yet you take up shields and spears (that is, go to war) — can this be called filial? As a subject you would slay your sovereign — can this be called loyal?” The guards wished to kill them, but Jiang Taigong said: “These are men of righteousness.” So the guards did them no harm, but drove them away. King Wu assembled eight hundred feudal lords at Mengjin, and after crossing the river joined battle with King Zhou's army at Muye. King Zhou was defeated because his troops turned their weapons about in the front ranks, and he burned himself on the Deer Terrace, and the Shang dynasty perished. Bo Yi and Shu Qi, ashamed to eat the grain of Zhou, withdrew to Mount Shouyang, where they gathered wild vetch to eat. A woman said: “You, sirs, in your righteousness will not eat the grain of Zhou — yet this vetch too is a plant of Zhou.” The two, shamed and indignant, refused all food and died, and were buried on Mount Shouyang.

They entered Shaolin Temple on Mount Song and paid homage to the First Patriarch, Bodhidharma. Reaching Luoyang, they saw the Sutra-Burning Terrace, the White Horse Temple, and other sights of the ancient capital.

The two of them reached Hedong in the ninth month. When the Prince of Shanyin heard that the canon was about to arrive, he led the various princes of the imperial clan, with banners, canopies, music, incense, and flowers, to welcome the scriptures into his palace. Miaofeng told the Prince of Shanyin: “The Master Chengyin whom you have been speaking of all this while
(Chengyin was the courtesy name of Master Hanshan)

has now come here as well.” The Prince of Shanyin was overjoyed, and at once asked to see the Master first, and only afterwards attended to the housing of the canon. The Prince kept the Master for the winter, asking him to stay within the prince's residence, where they sat facing each other at all hours, investigating the essential purport of the Surangama Sutra.
At that time the prefect of Shanyin, Lord Chen, was preparing to print the Zhongwu Collected Explanations of the Zhaolun and asked Master Hanshan to collate it. In former days, in the Zhaolun

On the Immutability of Things, the Master had not understood the essential meaning of “a whirlwind topples the mountains”; his doubt about this principle had lasted a long time, and now, reading it again, he still felt bewildered.

[The Whirlwind Topples the Mountains] The passage in the treatise reads: “The whirlwind topples the mountains, yet all is ever still; the rivers race and pour, yet they do not flow; the wild horses toss and drum, yet they do not move; the sun and moon traverse the sky, yet they do not go round.” (Translation: a fierce wind fells the mountains, yet all is ever still; the rivers race and pour, yet they do not flow; the dust tosses and drums, yet it does not move; the sun and moon march through the sky, yet they neither rise nor set.) The phrases in it — “the whirlwind topples the mountains,” “the rivers race and pour,” “the wild horses toss and drum,” “the sun and moon traverse the sky” — are surface appearances (appearances of the world). Yet seen from the true reality of all dharmas, the whirlwind, the rivers, the wild horses, and the sun and moon do not exist at all (originally there is not a single thing); where then could there be any toppling of mountains, racing and pouring, tossing and drumming, or traversing the sky? Therefore it is said: ever still, never flowing, never moving, never going round. (See in full
The True Reality of All Dharmas

, the article.) [Whirlwind] Also called the Pilan wind, rendered as: a great fierce wind. This is the great fierce wind that arises at the time of the kalpa-disaster. [Kalpa-disaster] The three disasters of fire, water, and wind that arise at the end of the kalpa of destruction; these three disasters sweep away the entire world. [The whirlwind topples the mountains] The great fierce wind of the kalpa-disaster blows down Mount Sumeru. [Wild horses] A metaphor for dust. It means that in the season of spring, when the yang energy stirs, one gazes far off at the dust in the marshes and grassy wilds and it seems like galloping horses; hence it is called “wild horses.”

Later, when he read: “The brahmacārin left home to cultivate, and only returned when his hair had turned white. The neighbors saw him and asked: ‘Is the brahmacārin of former days still here?’ The brahmacārin answered: ‘I look like the brahmacārin of former days, but I am not the brahmacārin of former days!’” — he suddenly awakened to the immutability of all dharmas
(all dharmas are from the first neither born nor extinguished, neither coming nor going)

, and he at once exclaimed with feeling: “This is a truth worthy of deep faith! All things whatsoever, in their essential nature, are from the first without birth or death, without coming or going, but forever abide.” He got down from the meditation couch to pay homage to the Buddha, and though he bowed up and down, no mark of rising or falling could be grasped. He lifted the bamboo blind and stepped out to stand on the terrace, when suddenly a cool wind blew through the leaves of the trees in the courtyard; it was the golden season of autumn, and flying leaves filled the sky, yet in the Master's mind no mark of movement could be grasped either. The Master thought: “This is precisely the state of ‘the whirlwind topples the mountains, yet all is ever still!’” Later, when he urinated and saw no mark of flowing, he thought: “This is like ‘the rivers race and pour, yet they do not flow!’” Thus the mass of doubt about birth and death melted away like ice, and he wrote a verse to express what his mind had understood: “Birth and death, day and night, water runs and flowers fall; today at last I know — the nostrils turn downward, after all”
(it has always been so, and never changed. Chan Master Fanyuan Cong said: “From the first the nostrils hang downward.” The Complete Five Lamps Record)
The next day Master Miaofeng came to see him and asked with delight: “Brother! Have you gained anything in your practice of late?” The Master answered: “In the night I saw two iron oxen by the river
(existence and nonexistence, coming and going, movement and stillness, birth and death)
fighting each other
, and both went into the water
(the two opposites are both extinguished)
, and to this day there is no news of them
(entering the gate of non-duality)
.” Master Miaofeng laughed and said: “Now you have the capital to dwell in the mountains!”
Not long afterwards the Prince of Shanyin invited Chan Master Faguang of Mount Funiu. The Master had long admired Master Faguang by reputation, and the moment they met their conversation

was wholly in accord. The Master then sought his instruction, and Chan Master Faguang expounded the Chan method of investigation — “investigate apart from mind, intellect, and consciousness; study beyond the paths of ordinary and sage” — and the Master grasped its subtle purport deeply. Only then did the Master understand that one who has awakened and clarified the mind-ground speaks words utterly different from ordinary people's, and he admired Chan Master Faguang all the more.

One day Chan Master Faguang found a few poems in the Master's bag, and after reading them said with feeling: “Such subtle and excellent lines — how did you come to write them?” Then he laughed and said: “Good they are, but the one step beyond is still not penetrated!” The Master asked: “Has the Master penetrated that step?” Chan Master Faguang said: “For thirty years I caught dragons and seized tigers; today a rabbit runs out of the grass and gives me a fright.” The Master said: “The Master is no dragon-catching, tiger-seizing hand.” Hearing this, Chan Master Faguang lifted his staff to strike the Master; the Master at once caught hold of the staff, and with his other hand stroked the master's beard, saying: “You speak of a rabbit, but it is a toad
(Master Hanshan's jest, meaning that he himself talks big)
.” The Chan master heard this and went off with a laugh.

Once Chan Master Faguang said to the Master: “You need not go elsewhere; shall we cultivate together on Mount Funiu?” The Master said: “In Dharma and in dialectic I see no gap between you and Chan Master Dahui; but in your daily behavior there seems to be something of the madman — reciting poems and matching couplets, your hand and mouth never resting. What is this about?” The Chan master answered: “This is my Chan sickness. When I first awakened, verses poured from me like a stream, day and night without cease, and I could not control them; afterwards it became this morbid state.” The Master asked again: “How is the Chan sickness to be treated when it first arises?” The Chan master said: “When the Chan sickness first arises, if you cannot see through it yourself, you must find a man of great eye and great skill to give you a sound beating, and then sleep soundly once; when you wake, the Chan sickness is gone. I regret that in those years, when my Chan sickness first arose, I had no clear-eyed expert to point the way, and so it came to this.”

In the first month of the new year the Master was to go to Mount Wutai. When the Chan master learned of it he wrote a poem to present to him, in which were the two lines “The lion in the snow — I ride it here to see you; the hidden dragon in the cave — let it go free.” He asked the Master: “Do you know what they mean?” The Master said: “No.” The Chan master explained: “What the poem means is that you should not clutch a dead snake.” The Master nodded in agreement. For a long time the Chan gate had lacked masters, and only after meeting Chan Master Faguang did the Master come to know what the methods of the school really were.

blocks.text: 8. Realizing the Way at Mount Wutai

inline.s: In the third year of Wanli (

), the Master was thirty. In the first month of that new year he set out from Hedong with Master Miaofeng for Mount Wutai, and only on the fifteenth day of the twelfth month, at the year's end, did they climb Mount Wutai. Dharma Master Dafang of the Great Pagoda Temple asked the two masters to choose a place to live at Longmen on the North Terrace; it was the most secluded and precipitous of spots. On the third day of the third month of the following year the Master cleared several old rooms out of the snowdrifts, and he and Master Miaofeng settled there.
